By exploring effective hamiltonians for these decays that have next-to-leading order corrections known, the authors provide a comprehensive update on parameters associated with various phenomenological implications of these calculations. Additionally, they include recent information about the top quark discovery and its impact on values of multiple parameters.

The work focuses on reducing theoretical uncertainties related to renormalization scale ambiguities by incorporating next-to-leading order corrections, and showcases the impact this improvement has on the determination of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix in several scenarios.

title: Heavy-fermion systems
abstract: Since the discovery by Steglich et al. (1979) of superconductivity in the high-effective-mass ($\ensuremath{\sim}200{m}_{e}$) electrons in Ce${\mathrm{Cu}}_{2}$${\mathrm{Si}}_{2}$, the search for and characterization of such "heavy-fermion" systems has been a rapidly growing field of study. The eight heavy-fermion systems known to date include superconductors (Ce${\mathrm{Cu}}_{2}$${\mathrm{Si}}_{2}$, U${\mathrm{Be}}_{13}$, U${\mathrm{Pt}}_{3}$), magnets (Np${\mathrm{Be}}_{13}$, ${\mathrm{U}}_{2}$${\mathrm{Zn}}_{17}$, U${\mathrm{Cd}}_{11}$), and materials in which no ordering is observed (Ce${\mathrm{Al}}_{3}$, Ce${\mathrm{Cu}}_{6}$). These $f$-electron materials have, in comparison to normal metals, enormous specific heat $\ensuremath{\gamma}$ values (450-1600 mJ/mol ${\mathrm{K}}^{2}$), large values of the low-temperature magnetic susceptibility $\ensuremath{\chi}$ (8-50\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}${10}^{\ensuremath{-}3}$ emu/mol G), maxima in the resistivity at low temperatures with large ${\ensuremath{\rho}}_{max}$ values (100-200 \ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\Omega} cm), and unusual temperature dependences of their specific heats below 10 K. The three heavy-fermion superconductors show such unusual behavior that the possibility of $p$-wave pairing of the superconducting electrons, rather than the usual BCS $s$-wave pairing, cannot be ruled out. This paper reviews the experimental results to date, to serve both as a status report and as a starting point for future research. Several correlations between properties are pointed out, including the observation that a low value of the Wilson ratio ($\ensuremath{\sim}\frac{\ensuremath{\chi}}{\ensuremath{\gamma}}$) appears to correlate with the occurrence of superconductivity.

Headline: "Revisiting 'Heavy-Fermion' Systems: A Deep Dive into Superconductivity and Unusual Pairing"

The three heavy-fermion superconductors show such unusual behavior that the possibility of p-wave pairing, rather than the conventional BCS s-wave pairing, cannot be ruled out. abstract: Nine experiments of timed odd-even judgments examined how parity and number magnitude are accessed from Arabic and verbal numerals. With Arabic numerals, Ss used the rightmost digit to access a store of semantic number knowledge. Verbal numerals went through an additional stage of transcoding to base 10. Magnitude information was automatically accessed from Arabic numerals. Large numbers preferentially elicited a rightward response, and small numbers a leftward response. The Spatial-Numerical Association of Response Codes (SNARC) effect depended only on relative number magnitude and was weaker or absent with letters or verbal numerals. Direction did not vary with handedness or hemispheric dominance but was linked to the direction of writing, as it faded or even reversed in right-to-left writing Iranian Ss

abstract: JADE (Java Agent Development Framework) is a software framework to make easy the development of multi-agent applications in compliance with the FIPA specifications. JADE can then be considered a middle-ware that implements an efficient agent platform and supports the development of multi agent systems. JADE agent platform tries to keep high the performance of a distributed agent system implemented with the Java language. In particular, its communication architecture tries to offer flexible and efficient messaging, transparently choosing the best transport available and leveraging state-of-the-art distributed object technology embedded within Java runtime environment. JADE uses an agent model and Java implementation that allow good runtime efficiency, software reuse, agent mobility and the realization of different agent architectures.

title: Final report of the E821 muon anomalous magnetic moment measurement at BNL
abstract: We present the final report from a series of precision measurements of the muon anomalous magnetic moment, a(mu)=(g-2)/2. The details of the experimental method, apparatus, data taking, and analysis are summarized. Data obtained at Brookhaven National Laboratory, using nearly equal samples of positive and negative muons, were used to deduce a(mu)(Expt)=11659208.0(5.4)(3.3)x10(-10), where the statistical and systematic uncertainties are given, respectively. The combined uncertainty of 0.54 ppm represents a 14-fold improvement compared to previous measurements at CERN. The standard model value for a(mu) includes contributions from virtual QED, weak, and hadronic processes. While the QED processes account for most of the anomaly, the largest theoretical uncertainty, approximate to 0.55 ppm, is associated with first-order hadronic vacuum polarization. Present standard model evaluations, based on e(+)e(-) hadronic cross sections, lie 2.2-2.7 standard deviations below the experimental result.
summary: Scientists from around the world publish final results of the E821 experiment at Brookhaven National Laboratory, which measures the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon - a fundamental subatomic particle. The newly determined value, a(mu) = 11659208.0 ± 5.4 (statistical uncertainty) ± 3.3 (systematic uncertainty) x 10-10, represents a significant improvement of 14 times compared to previous measurements at CERN. The discrepancy between the experimental result and the standard model evaluation for a(mu), primarily driven by hadronic vacuum polarization, is over 2 standard deviations, suggesting potential new physics beyond the Standard Model may be needed.

title: Equation of state of nucleon matter and neutron star structure
abstract: Properties of dense nucleon matter and the structure of neutron stars are studied using variational chain summation methods and the new Argonne v18 two-nucleon interaction. The neutron star gravitational mass limit obtained with this interaction is 1.67 M_{solar}. Boost corrections to the two-nucleon interaction, which give the leading relativistic effect of order (v/c)^2, as well as three-nucleon interactions, are also included in the nuclear Hamiltonian. Their successive addition increases the mass limit to 1.80 and 2.20 M_{solar}. Hamiltonians including a three-nucleon interaction predict a transition in neutron star matter to a phase with neutral pion condensation at a baryon number density of 0.2 fm^{-3}. We also investigate the possibility of dense nucleon matter having an admixture of quark matter, described using the bag model equation of state. Neutron stars of 1.4 M_{solar} do not appear to have quark matter admixtures in their cores. However, the heaviest stars are predicted to have cores consisting of a quark and nucleon matter mixture. These admixtures reduce the maximum mass of neutron stars from 2.20 to 2.02 (1.91) M_{solar} for bag constant B = 200 (122) MeV/fm^3. Stars with pure quark matter in their cores are found to be unstable. We also consider the possibility that matter is maximally incompressible above an assumed density, and show that realistic models of nuclear forces limit the maximum mass of neutron stars to be below 2.5 M_{solar}. The effects of the phase transitions on the composition of neutron star matter and its adiabatic index are discussed.
summary:
Physics Paper Predicts Mix of Quark and Nucleon Matter in Neutron Stars

A new study published in Physical Review C offers insight into the structure of neutron stars, utilizing advanced variational chain summation methods and the Argonne v18 two-nucleon interaction. The research suggests that dense nucleon matter could contain an admixture of quark matter, a significant shift in understanding the composition of the densest objects in the universe.

The study finds that Neutron stars with masses up to 1.4 M_solar do not appear to have quark matter admixtures in their cores. However, the heaviest stars are predicted to have cores consisting of a mixture of quark and nucleon matter. This admixture, according to the paper, reduces the maximum mass of neutron stars, potentially from 2.20 M_solar to as low as 2.02 (1.91) M_solar, depending on the bag constant. The findings also indicate that pure quark matter in a neutron star's core could lead to instability.

The authors explore other theories as well, including the possibility of matter becoming maximally incompressible above a certain density, and discuss how such phase transitions affect the composition and adiabatic index of neutron star matter. The research offers valuable contributions to understanding the mysterious realm of neutron stars.

title: Symmetries of Baryons and Mesons
abstract: The system of strongly interacting particles is discussed, with electromagnetism, weak interactions, and gravitation considered as perturbations. The electric current jα, the weak current Jα, and the gravitational tensor θαβ are all well-defined operators, with finite matrix elements obeying dispersion relations. To the extent that the dispersion relations for matrix elements of these operators between the vacuum and other states are highly convergent and dominated by contributions from intermediate one-meson states, we have relations like the Goldberger-Treiman formula and universality principles like that of Sakurai according to which the ρ meson is coupled approximately to the isotopic spin. Homogeneous linear dispersion relations, even without subtractions, do not suffice to fix the scale of these matrix elements; in particular, for the nonconserved currents, the renormalization factors cannot be calculated, and the universality of strength of the weak interactions is undefined. More information than just the dispersion relations must be supplied, for example, by field-theoretic models; we consider, in fact, the equal-time commutation relations of the various parts of j4 and J4. These nonlinear relations define an algebraic system (or a group) that underlies the structure of baryons and mesons. It is suggested that the group is in fact U(3)×U(3), exemplified by the symmetrical Sakata model. The Hamiltonian density θ44 is not completely invariant under the group; the noninvariant part transforms according to a particular representation of the group; it is possible that this information also is given correctly by the symmetrical Sakata model. Various exact relations among form factors follow from the algebraic structure. In addition, it may be worthwhile to consider the approximate situation in which the strangeness-changing vector currents are conserved and the Hamiltonian is invariant under U(3); we refer to this limiting case as "unitary symmetry." In the limit, the baryons and mesons form degenerate supermultiplets, which break up into isotopic multiplets when the symmetry-breaking term in the Hamiltonian is "turned on." The mesons are expected to form unitary singlets and octets; each octet breaks up into a triplet, a singlet, and a pair of strange doublets. The known pseudoscalar and vector mesons fit this pattern if there exists also an isotopic singlet pseudoscalar meson χ0. If we consider unitary symmetry in the abstract rather than in connection with a field theory, then we find, as an attractive alternative to the Sakata model, the scheme of Ne'eman and Gell-Mann, which we call the "eightfold way"; the baryons N, Λ, Σ, and Ξ form an octet, like the vector and pseudoscalar meson octets, in the limit of unitary symmetry. Although the violations of unitary symmetry must be quite large, there is some hope of relating certain violations to others. As an example of the methods advocated, we present a rough calculation of the rate of K+→μ++ν in terms of that of π+→μ++ν.
summary:
**Groundbreaking Physics Study Offers Insights on Baryons and Mesons**

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review, renowned physicist Murray Gell-Mann discusses the system of strongly interacting particles, proposing that algebraic structures underlying baryons and mesons can be defined by a group – suggested to be U(3)×U(3). The paper builds upon previous work, including Goldberger-Treiman formula and Sakurai's universality principles.

Gell-Mann argues that the system of electromagnetism, weak interactions, and gravitation can be viewed as perturbations. His findings suggest that baryons and mesons conform to a pattern seen in Ne'eman and Gell-Mann's "eightfold way," with an octet of baryons forming in the limit of unitary symmetry, much like the vector and pseudoscalar meson octets.

However, the violations of unitary symmetry are expected to be quite large, leaving open questions regarding their relationship. As an example, Gell-Mann presents a preliminary calculation of the rate of K+→μ++ν in relation to that of π+→μ++ν, demonstrating the novel methods he advocates in this study.

abstract: Continuing the program developed in a previous paper, a "superconductive" solution describing the proton-neutron doublet is obtained from a nonlinear spinor field Lagrangian. title: Review of particle physics. Particle Data Group
abstract: This biennial Review summarizes much of Particle Physics. Using data from previous editions plus new measurements from papers we list evaluate and average measured properties of gauge bosons leptons quarks mesons and baryons. We also summarize searches for hypothetical particles such as Higgs bosons heavy neutrinos and supersymmetric particles. All the particle properties and search limits are listed in Summary Tables. We also give numerous tables gures formulae and reviews of topics such as the Standard Model particle detectors probability and statistics. Among the reviews are many that are new or heavily revised including those on neutrino mixing CP violation in K D and B mesons Vcb the new exotic  particle extra dimensions grand unified theories cosmic background radiation dark matter cosmological parameters and big bang cosmology. A booklet is available containing the Summary Tables and abbreviated versions of some of the other sections of this full Review. All tables listings and reviews and errata are also available on the Particle Data Group website https://pdg.lbl.gov.
summary:

"Revised Particle Physics Review offers updated data on gauge bosons, Higgs bosons, and more

In a comprehensive biennial review published by the esteemed Particle Data Group in arXiv (Cornell University), over 50 renowned physicists provide an update on the properties of various particles within particle physics. The review also covers searches for hypothetical particles such as Higgs bosons, heavy neutrinos, and supersymmetric particles, listing all relevant properties and search limits in Summary Tables. In addition to these tables, the review features numerous charts, formulas, and reviews of various topics including the Standard Model, particle detectors, probability, statistics, and more.

Some of the updated sections within this meticulous review include a deep dive into neutrino mixing, CP violation in K D and B mesons, Vcb, exotic particles, extra dimensions, grand unified theories, cosmic background radiation, dark matter, cosmological parameters, and big bang cosmology. A booklet containing the Summary Tables and select sections of this extensive review is available at particle data group's website – <https://pdg.lbl.gov>.

title: Neutrino masses and mixings in gauge models with spontaneous parity violation
abstract: Unified electroweak gauge theories based on the gauge group $\mathrm{SU}{(2)}_{L}\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}\mathrm{SU}{(2)}_{R}\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}\mathrm{U}{(1)}_{B\ensuremath{-}L}$, in which the breakdown of parity invariance is spontaneous, lead most naturally to a massive neutrino. Assuming the neutrino to be a Majorana particle, we show that smallness of its mass can be understood as a result of the observed maximality of parity violation in low-energy weak interactions. This result is shown to be independent of the number of generations and unaffected by renormalization effects. Phenomenological consequences of this model at low energies are studied. Observation of neutrinoless double-$\ensuremath{\beta}$ decay will provide a crucial test of this class of models. Implications for rare decays such as $\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}e\ensuremath{\gamma}$, $\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}\mathrm{ee}\overline{e}$, etc. are also noted. It is pointed out that in the realm of neutral-current phenomena, departure from the predictions of the standard model for polarized-electron-hadron scattering, forward-backward asymmetry in ${e}^{+}{e}^{\ensuremath{-}}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}{\ensuremath{\mu}}^{+}{\ensuremath{\mu}}^{\ensuremath{-}}$, and neutrino interactions has a universal character and may be therefore used as a test of the model.

In an article published in Physical Review D, renowned physicists Rabindra N. Mohapatra and Goran Senjanović explore a new class of unified electroweak gauge theories. These theories aim to explain the massiveness of neutrinos by suggesting that their smallness stems from the observed maximality of parity violation in low-energy weak interactions. The researchers illustrate how this result is independent of the number of generations and remains unaffected by renormalization effects. They also discuss potential implications for rare decays, such as muon convertibility into electron and photons, and note that observing neutrinoless double-beta decay could serve as a crucial test of these models. Furthermore, they point out unique possibilities for neutral-current phenomena in polarized-electron-hadron scattering, forward-backward asymmetry in positron-electron collisions, and neutrino interactions, which could serve as evidence supporting this novel approach to the electroweak interaction.

Vollhardt propose a simplified method for studying correlations among fermions in an infinite number of dimensions using the Hubbard model. The approach promises to make diagnostic treatments substantially easier than in finite dimensions. Interestingly, the weak-coupling correlation energy in the infinite-dimensional setting is found to resemble that in 3 dimensions quite closely. Moreover, the authors' exact evaluation of explicit variational wave functions in this high-dimensional space recovers recent approximations based on slave-boson techniques, offering a new direction for understanding the behavior of fermions in complex settings.

title: Fluctuations in the New Inflationary Universe
abstract: The spectrum of density perturbations is calculated in the new-inflationary-universe scenario. The main source is the quantum fluctuations of the Higgs field, which lead to fluctuations in the time at which the false vacuum energy is released. The value of $\frac{\ensuremath{\delta}\ensuremath{\rho}}{\ensuremath{\rho}}$ on any given length scale $l$, at the time when the Hubble radius $\ensuremath{\gg}l$, is estimated. This quantity is nearly scale invariant (as desired), but is unfortunately about ${10}^{5}$ times too large.

title: Rigorous QCD analysis of inclusive annihilation and production of heavy quarkonium
abstract: A rigorous QCD analysis of the inclusive annihilation decay rates of heavy quarkonium states is presented. The effective-field-theory framework of nonrelativistic QCD is used to separate the short-distance scale of annihilation, which is set by the heavy quark mass M, from the longer-distance scales associated with quarkonium structure. The annihilation decay rates are expressed in terms of nonperturbative matrix elements of 4-fermion operators in nonrelativistic QCD, with coefficients that can be computed using perturbation theory in the coupling constant \\alpha_s(M). The matrix elements are organized into a hierarchy according to their scaling with v, the typical velocity of the heavy quark. An analogous factorization formalism is developed for the production cross sections of heavy quarkonium in processes involving momentum transfers of order M or larger. The factorization formulas are applied to the annihilation decay rates and production cross sections of S-wave states at next-to-leading order in v^2 and P-wave states at leading order in v^2.
summary:
Title: New QCD Analysis Offers Insights into Heavy Quarkonium Annihilation and Production

In a new paper published in Physical Review D, physicists Geoffrey T. Bodwin, Eric Braaten, and G. Peter Lepage have presented a rigorous analysis of the inclusive annihilation decay rates of heavy quarkonium states using Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) theory. The researchers employ an effective-field-theory framework called nonrelativistic QCD to separate short-distance scales related to heavy quark mass from longer-distance ones concerning quarkonium structure.

The focus of this work lies in the broader area of particle physics and the study of quarkonium, a type of bound state consisting of a heavy quark and an antiquark. The authors' analysis provides essential insights into the annihilation processes involving these states and delves into their production cross sections in high-momentum transfer scenarios. Their findings contribute to understanding the complex interplay between short and long distance aspects in the context of heavy quarkonium, paving the way for further investigations on this important topic in physics research.

abstract: We recently proposed a solution to the hierarchy problem not relying on low-energy supersymmetry or technicolor. Title: New Theories Suggest Sub-millimeter Dimensions for TeV Quantum Gravity

Summary:
The physicists Nima Arkani–Hamed, Savas Dimopoulos, and Gia Dvali propose a novel solution to the long-standing hierarchy problem in particle physics, one that doesn't rely on low-energy supersymmetry or technicolor. Instead, they propose that quantum gravity could be brought down to the TeV scale due to the presence of multiple (n ≥ 2) new sub-millimeter dimensions. The team explores the experimental viability of this scenario in a recent paper published in Physical Review D. The theories with more than two dimensions are immune to constraints, while for n = 2, the six-dimensional Planck scale must be pushed above about 30 TeV to avoid conflicts with supernova events and distortions of the cosmic microwave background. This research offers a fresh perspective in the quest to reconcile particle physics and quantum gravity.

title: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (in "The Review of Particle Properties" 2004)
abstract: A critical review is given of the current status of cosmological nucleosynthesis. In the framework of the standard model with 3 types of relativistic neutrinos, the baryon-to-photon ratio, η, corresponding to the inferred primordial abundances of helium-4 and lithium-7 is presently ~2 σbelow the value implied by the abundance of deuterium. The latter value is also coincident with the independent determination of ηfrom WMAP observations of CMB anisotropy. However taking systematic uncertainties in the abundance estimates into account, there is overall concordance in the range η= (3.4 - 6.9) x 10^{-10} @ 95% c.l. corresponding to a cosmological baryon density Ω_B h^2 = 0.012 - 0.025. If the above discrepancy is due to a neutrino chemical potential, then upto 7.1 effective neutrino species are allowed by nucleosynthesis. Other constraints on new physics are briefly discussed.
summary:
Title: A Cosmic Puzzle Unveiled: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and Neutrinos

Authors Brian D. Fields and Sarkar, in a recent study published in the arXiv (Cornell University), have delved into the realm of cosmic nucleosynthesis – revisiting the formation of elements soon after the Big Bang. The paper focuses on the baffling discrepancy between the inferred primordial abundances of helium-4, lithium-7 and deuterium.

The study suggests that the amount of baryonic matter in the universe, as indicated by deuterium abundance, is not in alignment with the traditional estimates of the baryon-to-photon ratio, η – a difference approximately 2σ below the expected value. However, accounting for systematic uncertainties in abundance estimates across various elements, the data falls within the range η = (3.4 - 6.9) x 10^{-10} with a 95% confidence level. This translates to a cosmological baryon density of Ω_B h^2 = 0.012 – 0.025.

The potential explanation offered by the researchers is a non-zero neutrino chemical potential, which could account for up to 7.1 additional effective neutrino species beyond the standard three. The paper also touches on other avenues of exploring new physics that may shed light on this intriguing astronomical mystery.

abstract: This biennial review summarizes much of Particle Physics. title: Observation of Electron-Antineutrino Disappearance at Daya Bay
abstract: The Daya Bay Reactor Neutrino Experiment has measured a nonzero value for the neutrino mixing angle θ(13) with a significance of 5.2 standard deviations. Antineutrinos from six 2.9 GWth reactors were detected in six antineutrino detectors deployed in two near (flux-weighted baseline 470 m and 576 m) and one far (1648 m) underground experimental halls. With a 43,000 ton-GWth-day live-time exposure in 55 days, 10,416 (80,376) electron-antineutrino candidates were detected at the far hall (near halls). The ratio of the observed to expected number of antineutrinos at the far hall is R=0.940±0.011(stat.)±0.004(syst.). A rate-only analysis finds sin(2)2θ(13)=0.092±0.016(stat.)±0.005(syst.) in a three-neutrino framework.
summary:
Title: groundbreaking physics study observes neutrino 'disappearance' at Daya Bay

A team of international researchers, led by Fengpeng An, have made a significant discovery in the field of particle physics with their study on the "Observation of Electron-Antineutrino Disappearance at Daya Bay." The experiment, published in Physical Review Letters, builds upon previous work involving the mixing angle θ13.

By measuring a nonzero value for this mixing angle with a significance of 5.2 standard deviations, the team found that antineutrinos from nuclear reactors appear to "disappear" when traveling longer distances—a phenomenon attributed to neutrino oscillation. This observation offers new insights into our understanding of the mysterious particle known as the electron neutrino and its role in fundamental physics.

title: FLUCTUATING ASYMMETRY: Measurement, Analysis, Patterns
abstract: With these words Darwin opened a brief paragraph citing observations antithetical to his supposition: anecdotal reports of the inheritance of characters missing from one side of the body. His initial hunch, however, has stood the test of time: Genetic studies have confirmed that where only small, random deviations from bilateral symmetry exist, the deviations in a particular direction have little or no measurable heritability (17, 47, 51, 65a, 73a, 74, 91). The genetic basis of bilateral symmetry thus appears to differ fundamentally from that of virtually all other morphological features. Why, then, all the recent (and not so recent) interest in such minor, nondirectional deviations from bilateral symmetry [fluctuating asymmetry (FA); 60 cited in 99]? Four reasons. First, FA relates in a curious way to what is perhaps the major unsolved general problem in modem biology: the orderly expression of genotypes as complex, three-dimensional phenotypes. As was emphasized in a flurry of activity in the mid to late 1950s, and many times since, FA provides an appealing measure of 'developmental noise,' or minor environmentally induced departures from some ideal developmental program (101). Its appeal derives from an a priori knowledge of the ideal: perfect bilateral symmetry. For unilateral characters, the ideal is rarely known (but see 1, 2, and 59 for one possible approach). A second reason for interest in
summary:
Title: New Study Challenges Darwin's Theory on Symmetry: Asymmetry in Biology Remains a Puzzling Developmental Mystery

In a new paper published in the Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics, scientists A. Richard Palmer and Curtis Strobeck delve into the enigma of fluctuating asymmetry (FA), minor deviations from bilateral symmetry in organisms. Contrary to Darwin's initial hypothesis, these deviations appear to have little heritability, setting them apart from most other morphological features.

The paper offers four reasons for recent interest in FA: first, it provides a measure of 'developmental noise', or minor departures from an ideal developmental program. Second, unlike unilateral characters, FA has a known ideal: perfect bilateral symmetry. Third, understanding FA could shed light on one of modern biology's most pressing questions - the orderly expression of genotypes as complex phenotypes. Lastly, it offers insights into evolutionary adaptations and environmental impacts on biological development. The paper continues to explore these ideas and proposes potential future directions for research in this intriguing field.

title: Theory of the Fermi Interaction
abstract: The representation of Fermi particles by two-component Pauli spinors satisfying a second order differential equation and the suggestion that in β decay these spinors act without gradient couplings leads to an essentially unique weak four-fermion coupling. It is equivalent to equal amounts of vector and axial vector coupling with two-component neutrinos and conservation of leptons. (The relative sign is not determined theoretically.) It is taken to be "universal"; the lifetime of the μ agrees to within the experimental errors of 2%. The vector part of the coupling is, by analogy with electric charge, assumed to be not renormalized by virtual mesons. This requires, for example, that pions are also "charged" in the sense that there is a direct interaction in which, say, a π0 goes to π- and an electron goes to a neutrino. The weak decays of strange particles will result qualitatively if the universality is extended to include a coupling involving a Λ or Σ fermion. Parity is then not conserved even for those decays like K→2π or 3π which involve no neutrinos. The theory is at variance with the measured angular correlation of electron and neutrino in He6, and with the fact that fewer than 10^-4 pion decay into electron and neutrino.
summary:
**Feynman and Gell-Mann Propose Unique Fermi Interaction Theory**

Physicists Richard Feynman and Murray Gell-Mann present a novel theory on the interactions of Fermi particles in a paper published in Physical Review, suggesting that these particles can be represented by two-component Pauli spinors. In their proposed theory, Fermion particles exhibit both vector and axial vector couplings during beta decay, leading to a unique four-fermion weak interaction.

This interaction, which also ensures lepton conservation, is considered universally applicable in various particle decays. While the relative sign between vector and axial vector coupling remains undetermined theoretically, the authors hypothesize that the vector part of the coupling does not get renormalized by virtual mesons — a concept akin to electric charge.

The theory, when extended to involve particles like Λ or Σ fermions, promises to explain the decays of strange particles; however, it contradicts experimental findings on the angular correlation of electron and neutrino in He6 and underestimates pion decay into electron and neutrino by several orders of magnitude.

title: Resonant Optical Antennas
abstract: We have fabricated nanometer-scale gold dipole antennas designed to be resonant at optical frequencies. On resonance, strong field enhancement in the antenna feed gap leads to white-light supercontinuum generation. The antenna length at resonance is considerably shorter than one-half the wavelength of the incident light. This is in contradiction to classical antenna theory but in qualitative accordance with computer simulations that take into account the finite metallic conductivity at optical frequencies. Because optical antennas link propagating radiation and confined/enhanced optical fields, they should find applications in optical characterization, manipulation of nanostructures, and optical information processing.

title: Baryonic Features in the Matter Transfer Function
abstract: We provide scaling relations and tting formulae for adiabatic cold dark matter cosmologies that account for all baryon e ects in the matter transfer function to better than 10 % in the largescale structure regime. They are based upon a physically well-motivated separation of the e ects of acoustic oscillations, Compton drag, velocity overshoot, baryon infall, adiabatic damping, Silk damping, and cold-dark-matter growth suppression. We also nd a simpler, more accurate, and better motivated form for the zero baryon transfer function than previous works. These descriptions are employed to quantify the amplitude and location of baryonic features in linear theory. While baryonic oscillations are prominent if the baryon fraction Ωb=Ω0&gt; Ω0h 2 +0:2, the main e ect in more conventional cosmologies is a sharp suppression in the transfer function below the sound horizon. We provide a simple but accurate description of this e ect and stress that it is not well approximated by a change in the shape parameter Γ. summary:

Eisenstein and Wayne Hu propose new modeling methods for the Baryonic Features in the Matter Transfer Function, improving accuracy by up to 10% in large-structure cosmic studies. The innovative approach separates baryon effects like acoustic oscillations, velocity overshoot, and infall from dark matter growth, providing a more nuanced understanding of structure formation.

The groundbreaking work offers an updated description of the zero-baryon transfer function and quantifies linear-theory baryonic features in cosmological models with varying baryon fractions (Ωb ≥ Ω0h +0.2). With this new model, researchers can better analyze cosmic structure development in various universes, shedding light on both the dominant baryonic oscillations and the subtle yet significant suppression below the sound horizon in conventional cosmologies — findings not well-captured by the shape parameter Γ.

title: New parton distributions for collider physics
abstract: We extract new parton distribution functions (PDFs) of the proton by global analysis of hard scattering data in the general-mass framework of perturbative quantum chromodynamics. Our analysis includes new theoretical developments together with the most recent collider data from deep-inelastic scattering, vector boson production, and single-inclusive jet production. Due to the difficulty in fitting both the DO Run-II W lepton asymmetry data and some fixed-target DIS data, we present two families of PDFs, CT10 and CT10W, without and with these high-luminosity W lepton asymmetry data included in the global analysis. With both sets of PDFs, we study theoretical predictions and uncertainties for a diverse selection of processes at the Fermilab Tevatron and the CERN Large Hadron Collider.
summary:
Study Reveals New Parton Distribution Functions for Collider Physics

In a new paper published in Physical Review D, a team of scientists led by Hung-Liang Lai present their findings on new parton distribution functions (PDFs) of the proton. The study aims to better understand hard scattering data within the context of perturbative quantum chromodynamics.

The research incorporates recent experimental data from various collider sources, including deep-inelastic scattering, vector boson production, and single-inclusive jet production. Due to challenges in fitting certain Tevatron W lepton asymmetry data and some fixed-target DIS data, two families of PDFs—CT10 and CT10W—were developed, with the latter including high-luminosity W lepton asymmetry data for improved accuracy.

The scientists' work contributes to a deeper understanding of diverse processes at both the Fermilab Tevatron and the CERN Large Hadron Collider by examining theoretical predictions and uncertainties using these new parton distribution functions. This research paves the way for better interpretations of collider data and advancements in particle physics.

title: Purchasing Power Parity Tests in Cointegrated Panels
abstract: This paper employs recently developed techniques for testing hypotheses in cointegrated panels to test the strong version of purchasing power parity for a panel of post Bretton Woods data. We also introduce a new between-dimension dynamic OLS estimator and find that the between-dimension FMOLS and DOLS estimates of the long-run deviation from purchasing power parity are larger than the corresponding within-dimension estimates. Finally, we attempt to reconcile these rejections with the mixed findings that have been reported in panel unit root studies. © 2001 by the President and Fellows of Harvard College and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

title: Behavior of Current Divergences under<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>SU</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>SU</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>
abstract: We investigate the behavior under SU3×SU3 of the hadron energy density and the closely related question of how the divergences of the axial-vector currents and the strangeness-changing vector currents transform under SU3×SU3. We assume that two terms in the energy density break SU3×SU3 symmetry; under SU3 one transforms as a singlet, the other as the member of an octet. The simplest possible behavior of these terms under chiral transformations is proposed: They are assigned to a single (3,3*)+(3*,3) representation of SU3×SU3 and parity together with the current divergences. The commutators of charges and current divergences are derived in terms of a single constant c that describes the strength of the SU3-breaking term relative to the chiral symmetry-breaking term. The constant c is found not to be small, as suggested earlier, but instead close to the value (-sqrt[2]) corresponding to an SU2×SU2 symmetry, realized mainly by massless pions rather than parity doubling. Some applications of the proposed commutation relations are given, mainly to the pseudoscalar mesons, and other applications are indicated.
summary:
Headline: New Study Suggests Surprising Behavior of Particle Interactions in Physics

Summary:

The researchers suggest these terms are represented by a single (3,3*)+(3*,3) representation of SU3×SU3 and parity, along with the current divergences. The study derives commutation relations in terms of a constant 'c', which surprisingly is found to be closer to the value (-sqrt[2]) corresponding to an SU2×SU2 symmetry, rather than the previously suggested small values. The findings could have significant implications for our understanding of pseudoscalar mesons and other subatomic particles.

title: Non-Lagrangian Models of Current Algebra
abstract: An alternative is proposed to specific Lagrangian models of current algebra. In this alternative there are no explicit canonical fields, and operator products at the same point [say, ${j}_{\ensuremath{\mu}}(x){j}_{\ensuremath{\mu}}(x)$] have no meaning. Instead, it is assumed that scale invariance is a broken symmetry of strong interactions, as proposed by Kastrup and Mack. Also, a generalization of equal-time commutators is assumed: Operator products at short distances have expansions involving local fields multiplying singular functions. It is assumed that the dominant fields are the $\mathrm{SU}(3)\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}\mathrm{SU}(3)$ currents and the $\mathrm{SU}(3)\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}\mathrm{SU}(3)$ multiplet containing the pion field. It is assumed that the pion field scales like a field of dimension $\ensuremath{\Delta}$, where $\ensuremath{\Delta}$ is unspecified within the range $1\ensuremath{\le}\ensuremath{\Delta}<4$; the value of $\ensuremath{\Delta}$ is a consequence of renormalization. These hypotheses imply several qualitative predictions: The second Weinberg sum rule does not hold for the difference of the ${K}^{*}$ and axial-${K}^{*}$ propagators, even for exact $\mathrm{SU}(2)\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}\mathrm{SU}(2)$; electromagnetic corrections require one subtraction proportional to the $I=1$, ${I}_{z}=0\ensuremath{\sigma}$ field; $\ensuremath{\eta}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}3\ensuremath{\pi}$ and ${\ensuremath{\pi}}_{0}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}2\ensuremath{\gamma}$ are allowed by current algebra. Octet dominance of nonleptonic weak processes can be understood, and a new form of superconvergence relation is deduced as a consequence. A generalization of the Bjorken limit is proposed.

title: Chiral magnetic effect
abstract: Topological charge changing transitions can induce chirality in the quark-gluon plasma by the axial anomaly. We study the equilibrium response of the quark-gluon plasma in such a situation to an external magnetic field. To mimic the effect of the topological charge changing transitions we will introduce a chiral chemical potential. We will show that an electromagnetic current is generated along the magnetic field. This is the Chiral Magnetic Effect. We compute the magnitude of this current as a function of magnetic field, chirality, temperature, and baryon chemical potential.
summary:
Physical Review D publishes groundbreaking research on Chiral Magnetic Effect

The study explores the behavior of quark-gluon plasma in response to an external magnetic field, given a scenario where topological charge changing transitions induce chirality. To simulate this effect, they introduce a "chiral chemical potential." The team's findings show that an electromagnetic current is generated along the magnetic field—a phenomenon known as the Chiral Magnetic Effect. They have computed the magnitude of this current in relation to magnetic field strength, chirality, temperature, and baryon chemical potential, advancing our comprehension of this fascinating physical phenomenon.

title: Observational Evidence for Self-Interacting Cold Dark Matter
abstract: Cosmological models with cold dark matter composed of weakly interacting particles predict overly dense cores in the centers of galaxies and clusters and an overly large number of halos within the Local Group compared to actual observations. We propose that the conflict can be resolved if the cold dark matter particles are self-interacting with a large scattering cross section but negligible annihilation or dissipation. In this scenario, astronomical observations may enable us to study dark matter properties that are inaccessible in the laboratory.
summary:
**New Study Suggests Self-Interacting Cold Dark Matter Could Resolve Galaxy Density Puzzle**

Steinhardt propose a novel solution to a longstanding mystery in physics: the incongruity between theoretical predictions on dark matter and observational data of galactic clusters and the Local Group, a congregation of galaxies within our galaxy's vicinity.

The researchers contend that cold dark matter, traditionally perceived as non-interacting particles, could have substantial self-interactions with a high scattering cross section but nearly undetectable annihilation or dissipation. This intriguing hypothesis could open the door to studying exclusive properties of dark matter through astronomical observations, traditionally explored within laboratory settings.

title: Computing quark and gluon distribution functions for very large nuclei
abstract: We argue that the distribution functions for quarks and gluons are computable at small x for sufficiently large nuclei, perhaps larger than can be physically realized. For such nuclei, we argue that weak coupling methods may be used. We show that the computation of the distribution functions can be recast as a many body problem with a modified propagator, a coupling constant which depends on the multiplicity of particles per unit rapidity per unit area, and for non-abelian gauge theories, some extra media dependent vertices. We explicitly compute the distribution function for gluons to lowest order, and argue how they may be computed in higher order.
summary:
Scientific Paper Unveils Method for Calculating Quark and Gluon Distribution Functions in Large Nuclei

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review D, physicists Larry McLerran and Raju Venugopalan propose a novel approach to compute distribution functions for quarks and gluons within large nuclei. This study could potentially extend beyond realistic physical dimensions.

The researchers suggest that weak coupling methods can be applied to calculate these distribution functions in sufficiently large nuclei. They redefine the problem as a many-body issue with a modified propagator and a coupling constant that depends on the particle multiplicity per unit rapidity per unit area. For non-abelian gauge theories, they introduce additional media-dependent vertices. The team initially computes gluon distribution functions to the lowest order, providing insights into their higher-order computations as well.

title: Herwig++ physics and manual
abstract:
In this paper we describe 
$\mathsf{Herwig++}$ 
version 2.2, a general-purpose Monte Carlo event generator for the simulation of hard lepton-lepton and hadron-hadron collisions. A number of important hard scattering processes are available, together with an interface via the Les Houches Accord to specialized matrix element generators for additional processes. The simulation of Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) physics includes a range of models and allows new models to be added by encoding the Feynman rules of the model. The parton-shower approach is used to simulate initial- and final-state QCD radiation, including colour coherence effects, with special emphasis on the correct description of radiation from heavy particles. The underlying event is simulated using an eikonal multiple parton-parton scattering model. The formation of hadrons from the quarks and gluons produced in the parton shower is described using the cluster hadronization model. Hadron decays are simulated using matrix elements, where possible including spin correlations and off-shell effects.
summary:
New physics simulation tool unveiled: Scientists present version 2.2 of Herwig++, a comprehensive event generator for hard lepton and hadron collisions

In the latest edition of The European Physical Journal C, a team of researchers have introduced an updated version (2.2) of the general-purpose Monte Carlo event generator, Herwig++. This tool is used to simulate hard scattering processes in various particle collisions, including those beyond the Standard Model (BSM).

The new version includes enhancements that allow for a more accurate description of radiation from heavy particles and the formation of hadrons using advanced models like the cluster hadronization model. herwig++ also supports additional processes through an interface via the Les Houches Accord with specialized matrix element generators. Overall, this work contributes to advancing our understanding of particle physics beyond the Standard Model by providing an essential tool for simulations in high-energy collisions.

title: Finite-Temperature Field Theory
abstract: The 2006 second edition of this book develops the basic formalism and theoretical techniques for studying relativistic quantum field theory at high temperature and density. Specific physical theories treated include QED, QCD, electroweak theory, and effective nuclear field theories of hadronic and nuclear matter. Topics include: functional integral representation of the partition function, diagrammatic expansions, linear response theory, screening and plasma oscillations, spontaneous symmetry breaking, Goldstone theorem, resummation and hard thermal loops, lattice gauge theory, phase transitions, nucleation theory, quark-gluon plasma, and color superconductivity. Applications to astrophysics and cosmology cover white dwarf and neutron stars, neutrino emissivity, baryon number violation in the early universe, and cosmological phase transitions. Applications to relativistic nucleus-nucleus collisions are also included. The book is written for theorists in elementary particle physics, nuclear physics, astrophysics, and cosmology. Problems are given at the end of each chapter, and numerous references to the literature are included.
summary:
**New Physics Book Offers Insights on High-Temperature Quantum Field Theory**

Kapusta and Charles Gale present an updated book that delves into the study of Relativistic Quantum Field Theory at extreme temperatures and densities. The text explores various physical theories such as Quantum Electrodynamics (QED), Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), electroweak theory, and more in the context of particle physics and nuclear matter.

Topics covered in the book include functional integral representation of the partition function, diagrammatic expansions, linear response theory, screening and plasma oscillations, spontaneous symmetry breaking, and resummation techniques (hard thermal loops). The book also discusses phase transitions, nucleation theory, quark-gluon plasma, color superconductivity, and their connections to astrophysics, cosmology, white dwarfs, neutron stars, neutrino emissivity, baryon number violation in the early universe, and cosmological phase transitions. title: Observation of Reactor Electron Antineutrinos Disappearance in the RENO Experiment
abstract: The RENO experiment has observed the disappearance of reactor electron antineutrinos, consistent with neutrino oscillations, with a significance of 4.9 standard deviations. Antineutrinos from six 2.8 GW(th) reactors at the Yonggwang Nuclear Power Plant in Korea, are detected by two identical detectors located at 294 and 1383 m, respectively, from the reactor array center. In the 229 d data-taking period between 11 August 2011 and 26 March 2012, the far (near) detector observed 17102 (154088) electron antineutrino candidate events with a background fraction of 5.5% (2.7%). The ratio of observed to expected numbers of antineutrinos in the far detector is 0.920±0.009(stat)±0.014(syst). From this deficit, we determine sin(2)2θ(13)=0.113±0.013(stat)±0.019(syst) based on a rate-only analysis.
summary:
**Headline:**
Korean Experiment Confirms Oscillation of Electron Antineutrinos with High Precision

**Short Summary:**
A new study published in Physical Review Letters, led by a team of 27 Korean scientists, has confirmed the disappearance of reactor electron antineutrinos – a phenomenon known as neutrino oscillations – with a significant level of 4.9 standard deviations. The RENO experiment, conducted at the Yonggwang Nuclear Power Plant in South Korea, employed two identical detectors situated at different distances from the reactor array center. According to their findings, the far detector detected fewer electron antineutrino events than expected, which has been attributed to neutrino oscillations. The researchers used a rate-only analysis to determine the value of sin(2)2θ(13), a parameter crucial in understanding the behavior of these subatomic particles.

title: Atomic Scattering in the Presence of an External Confinement and a Gas of Impenetrable Bosons
abstract:
We calculate, within the pseudopotential approximation, a one-dimensional
scattering amplitude and effective one-dimensional interaction potential for
atoms confined transversally by an atom waveguide or highly elongated
``cigar''-shaped atomic trap. We show that in the low-energy scattering regime,
the scattering process degenerates to a total reflection suggesting an
experimental realization of a famous model in theoretical physics - a
one-dimensional gas of impenetrable bosons (``Tonks'' gas). We give an estimate
for suitable experimental parameters for alkali atoms confined in waveguides.
summary: In Physics, Maxim Olshanii examines the scattering behavior of atoms in one-dimensional channels or "cigar"-shaped traps. Using a pseudopotential approximation, he predicts a total reflection phenomenon in low-energy scattering that mirrors a well-known model in theoretical physics: a one-dimensional gas of impenetrable bosons, or Tonks gas. The study proposes experimentally viable parameters for alkali atoms to implement this intriguing scenario, potentially leading to new avenues in the study of atomic interaction and behavior.

title: String axiverse
abstract:
String theory suggests the simultaneous presence of many ultralight axions
possibly populating each decade of mass down to the Hubble scale 10^-33eV.
Conversely the presence of such a plenitude of axions (an "axiverse") would be
evidence for string theory, since it arises due to the topological complexity
of the extra-dimensional manifold and is ad hoc in a theory with just the four
familiar dimensions. We investigate how upcoming astrophysical experiments will
explore the existence of such axions over a vast mass range from 10^-33eV to
10^-10eV. Axions with masses between 10^-33eV to 10^-28eV cause a rotation of
the CMB polarization that is constant throughout the sky. The predicted
rotation angle is of order \alpha~1/137. Axions in the mass range 10^-28eV to
10^-18eV give rise to multiple steps in the matter power spectrum, that will be
probed by upcoming galaxy surveys. Axions in the mass range 10^-22eV to
10^-10eV affect the dynamics and gravitational wave emission of rapidly
rotating astrophysical black holes through the Penrose superradiance process.
When the axion Compton wavelength is of order of the black hole size, the
axions develop "superradiant" atomic bound states around the black hole
"nucleus". Their occupation number grows exponentially by extracting rotational
energy from the ergosphere, culminating in a rotating Bose-Einstein axion
condensate emitting gravitational waves. This mechanism creates mass gaps in
the spectrum of rapidly rotating black holes that diagnose the presence of
axions. The rapidly rotating black hole in the X-ray binary LMC X-1 implies an
upper limit on the decay constant of the QCD axion f_a<2*10^17GeV, much below
the Planck mass. This reach can be improved down to the grand unification scale
f_a<2*10^16GeV, by observing smaller stellar mass black holes.

New Study Explores Possibility of a "String Axiverse" Invisible Particles

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review D, researchers led by Asimina Arvanitaki propose the existence of a vast array of ultralight axions known as a "string axiverse." This research, which builds upon previous work in particle physics and axion theory, suggests that string theory may be validated by the presence of these extra axions.

The team investigates how upcoming astrophysical experiments could confirm the existence of such axions over a wide mass range from 10^-33eV to 10^-10eV. Axions in specific mass ranges impact components of cosmic microwave background polarization, matter power spectrum, and gravitational wave emission in rapidly rotating astrophysical black holes, providing unique opportunities for detection. The research provides insights into the potential implications, such as diagnosing the presence of axions and creating mass gaps in the spectrum of rapidly rotating black holes, which could revolutionize our understanding of dark matter and particle physics.

title: Axion cosmology
abstract: Axions comprise a broad class of particles that can play a major role in explaining the unknown aspects of cosmology. They are also well-motivated within high energy physics, appearing in theories related to CPCP-violation in the standard model, supersymmetric theories, and theories with extra-dimensions, including string theory, and so axion cosmology offers us a unique view onto these theories. I review the motivation and models for axions in particle physics and string theory. I then present a comprehensive and pedagogical view on the cosmology and astrophysics of axion-like particles, starting from inflation and progressing via BBN, the CMB, reionization and structure formation, up to the present-day Universe. Topics covered include: axion dark matter (DM); direct and indirect detection of axions, reviewing existing and future experiments; axions as dark radiation; axions and the cosmological constant problem; decays of heavy axions; axions and stellar astrophysics; black hole superradiance; axions and astrophysical magnetic fields; axion inflation, and axion DM as an indirect probe of inflation. A major focus is on the population of ultralight axions created via vacuum realignment, and its role as a DM candidate with distinctive phenomenology. Cosmological observations place robust constraints on the axion mass and relic density in this scenario, and I review where such constraints come from. I next cover aspects of galaxy formation with axion DM, and ways this can be used to further search for evidence of axions. An absolute lower bound on DM particle mass is established. It is View the MathML sourcema>10−24eV from linear observables, extending to View the MathML sourcema≳10−22eV from non-linear observables, and has the potential to reach View the MathML sourcema≳10−18eV in the future. These bounds are weaker if the axion is not all of the DM, giving rise to limits on the relic density at low mass. This leads to the exciting possibility that the effects of axion DM on structure formation could one day be detected, and the axion mass and relic density measured from cosmological observables.

The review places a strong emphasis on ultra light axions generated via vacuum realignment, which could potentially serve as a distinctive DM candidate with unique characteristics. Marsh discusses the constraints on axion mass and relic density imposed by cosmological observations, proposing that future observatories may reach even lower limits, potentially enabling the measurement of axion properties from cosmological data.

Intriguingly, Marsh suggests that the impact of axion DM on structure formation could one day be detected, offering the tantalizing prospect of directly measuring the axion mass and relic density from cosmic observations. title: Stark Effect in Rapidly Varying Fields
abstract: A method is developed for calculating the effects of a strong oscillating field on two states of a quantum-mechanical system which are connected by a matrix element of the field. Explicit approximate solutions are obtained for a variety of special cases, and the results of numerical computations are given for others. The effect of an rf field on the $J=2\ensuremath{\rightarrow}1$ $l$-type doublet microwave absorption lines of OCS has been studied in particular both experimentally and theoretically. Each line was observed to split into two components when the frequency of the rf field was near 12.78 Mc or 38.28 Mc, which are the frequencies separating the $J=1$ and $J=2$ pairs of levels, respectively. By measuring the rf frequency, ${\ensuremath{\nu}}_{0}$, at which the microwave lines are split into two equally intense components, one may determine the separation between the energy levels. The measured value of ${\ensuremath{\nu}}_{0}$ depends upon the intensity of the rf field and the form of this dependence has been calculated and found to be in good agreement with the experimental results.

abstract: We report on a search for weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) using 278.8 days of data collected with the XENON1T experiment at LNGS. title: Parametrization of the Kobayashi-Maskawa Matrix
abstract: The quark mixing matrix (Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix) is expanded in powers of a small parameter $\ensuremath{\lambda}$ equal to $sin{\ensuremath{\theta}}_{c}=0.22$. The term of order ${\ensuremath{\lambda}}^{2}$ is determined from the recently measured $B$ lifetime. Two remaining parameters, including the $\mathrm{CP}$-nonconservation effects, enter only the term of order ${\ensuremath{\lambda}}^{3}$ and are poorly constrained. A significant reduction in the limit on $\frac{{\ensuremath{\epsilon}}^{\ensuremath{'}}}{\ensuremath{\epsilon}}$ possible in an ongoing experiment would tightly constrain the $\mathrm{CP}$-nonconservation parameter and could rule out the hypothesis that the only source of $\mathrm{CP}$ nonconservation is the Kobayashi-Maskawa mechanism.
summary:

Wolfenstein's innovative work in Physical Review Letters focuses on the parametrization of the Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix, a key aspect of particle physics that helps us understand the behavior and mixing between different types of quarks. The study expands the matrix using a small parameter, $\lambda$ (approximately equivalent to $sin{\theta}_{c}=0.22$), and predicts values for terms up to order ${\lambda}^{2}$.

The critical next-level term, responsible for CP violation effects, remains unconstrained due to insufficient data. The experimental findings that could limit the ratio of CP-violation parameters $\frac{{\epsilon}^{\prime}}{\epsilon}$ would significantly tighten constraints on this mysterious parameter and potentially rule out the prevailing hypothesis suggesting that all CP nonconservation arises solely from the Kobayashi-Maskawa mechanism.

title: Shape effects in plasmon resonance of individual colloidal silver nanoparticles
abstract: We present a systematic study of the effect of size and shape on the spectral response of individual silver nanoparticles. An experimental method has been developed that begins with the detection and characterization of isolated nanoparticles in the optical far field. The plasmon resonance optical spectrum of many individual nanoparticles are then correlated to their size and shape using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy. We find that specific geometrical shapes give distinct spectral responses. In addition, inducing subtle changes in the particles’ morphology by heating causes a shift in the individual particle spectrum and provides a simple means of tuning the spectral response to a desired optical wavelength. Improved colloidal preparation methods could potentially lead to homogeneous populations of identical particle shapes and colors. These multicolor colloids could be used as biological labels, surface enhanced Raman scattering substrates, or near field optical microscopy sources covering the full range of wavelengths in the visible spectrum.

title: The Nambu—Jona-Lasinio model of quantum chromodynamics
abstract: The Nambu---Jona-Lasinio model is reviewed in its flavor SU(2) and SU(3) versions applied to quarks. The dynamical generation of quark masses is demonstrated as a feature of chiral symmetry breaking. One finds that the associated meson spectra, as well as the meson static properties, can be well described. Current-algebra results, which arise as a consequence of symmetry considerations, automatically hold for this model and are explicitly demonstrated to do so. These include the Goldberger-Treiman and Gell-Mann-Oakes-Renner relations. Effects of finite temperature, finite chemical potential, and strong Maxwell and chromoelectromagnetic fields on the dynamically generated quark mass and the meson spectra are discussed. The alternative procedure of bosonization to obtain an effective Lagrange density in mesonic degrees of freedom, using the derivative expansion, is also presented. The current status in relating the results of this model to that of chiral perturbation theory is critically examined.
summary:
In a new review published in Reviews of Modern Physics, scientist S. P. Klevansky delves into the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio (NJL) model, a critical tool in understanding quantum chromodynamics, particularly its SU(2) and SU(3) applications involving quarks. The paper highlights the model's key feature: dynamically generating quark masses due to chiral symmetry breaking.

The review also demonstrates that the associated meson spectra and static properties can be accurately described within this framework. Crucial results from current algebra, such as the Goldberger-Treiman and Gell-Mann-Oakes-Renner relations, are verified in the NJL model.

Furthermore, Klevansky discusses the impacts of temperature, chemical potential, strong Maxwell and chromoelectromagnetic fields on dynamically generated quark masses and meson spectra, underscoring this model's importance for exploring extreme physical conditions. The article concludes by exploring an alternative approach, bosonization, to derive an effective mesonic Lagrangian density and critically evaluates the connection between the NJL model results and those of chiral perturbation theory.

title: High-precision, charge-dependent Bonn nucleon-nucleon potential
abstract:
We present a charge-dependent nucleon-nucleon (NN) potential that fits the
world proton-proton data below 350 MeV available in the year of 2000 with a
chi^2 per datum of 1.01 for 2932 data and the corresponding neutron-proton data
with chi^2/datum = 1.02 for 3058 data. This reproduction of the NN data is more
accurate than by any phase-shift analysis and any other NN potential. The
charge-dependence of the present potential (that has been dubbed `CD-Bonn') is
based upon the predictions by the Bonn Full Model for charge-symmetry and
charge-independence breaking in all partial waves with J <= 4. The potential is
represented in terms of the covariant Feynman amplitudes for one-boson exchange
which are nonlocal. Therefore, the off-shell behavior of the CD-Bonn potential
differs in a characteristic and well-founded way from commonly used local
potentials and leads to larger binding energies in nuclear few- and many-body
systems, where underbinding is a persistent problem.
summary:
Title: Breakthrough in Nuclear Physics: High-precision Charge-Dependent Potential for Proton-Proton Interactions
Subhead: Paper in Physical Review C proposes charge-dependent Bonn nucleon-nucleon potential with high precision, improving upon existing phase-shift analyses and other potentials.

Summary: Renowned physicist R. Machleidt has introduced a new, highly precise charge-dependent nucleon-nucleon (NN) potential called CD-Bonn. This groundbreaking potential offers superior fit to world proton-proton data below 350 MeV from the year 2000, with a remarkable chi^2 per datum of just 1.01 for over 2900 data points. The neutron-proton data is also accurately reproduced with a similar chi^2 rating. The CD-Bonn potential's charge-dependence is grounded in predictions by the Bonn Full Model, and it differs from common local potentials through its covariant Feynman amplitudes for one-boson exchange, which are nonlocal. This distinction results in larger binding energies in nuclear few- and many-body systems, addressing a longstanding issue of underbinding in these complex systems.

title: First-order phase transition of a vacuum and the expansion of the Universe
abstract: The progress of a first-order phase transition of a vacuum in the expanding Universe is investigated. The expansion of bubbles of a stable vacuum is calculated simultaneously with the cosmic expansion with the aid of the following two simplified nucleation rates of bubbles <it>p</it>: (i) <it>p</it> = <it>p</it><inf>T</inf> T<inf>c</inf> <it>δ</it> (<it>T−T</it>c) in the hot Universe models, (ii) <it>p</it> = 0 for <it>n</it> > <it>n</it><inf>c</inf> and <it>p</it> = <it>p</it><inf>Q</inf> for <it>n</it> < <it>n</it><inf>c</inf> in the cold Universe models, where <it>T</it> is the cosmic temperature, <it>T</it><inf>c</inf> the critical temperature, <it>n</it> the cosmic number density of the fermions coupled to the order parameter of the vacuum, <it>n</it><inf>c</inf> the critical density, and <it>p</it><inf>T</inf> and <it>p</it><inf>Q</inf> are parameters. The following results are obtained: (1) If the nucleation rates are small and the vacuum stays at the metastable state for a long time, the Universe begins to expand exponentially. As a result, the progress of the phase transition is delayed more and more by the rapid cosmic expansion. In particular, in model (i), if <it>p</it><inf>T</inf> is less than a critical value, the phase transition never finishes. (2) The lower limits of the nucleation parameter <it>p</it><inf>T</inf> and <it>p</it><inf>Q</inf> are obtained from observation of the number ratio of photons to baryons in the present Universe. (3) If the phase transition of the vacuum in SU(5) GUT is of first order or if there exists a hypothetical first-order phase transition of the vacuum in the very early stage in which baryon number is not conserved, the density and the velocity fluctuations created by the phase transition may account for the origin of galaxies.

title: Hadron masses in a gauge theory
abstract: We explore the implications for hadron spectroscopy of the "standard" gauge model of weak, electromagnetic, and strong interactions. The model involves four types of fractionally charged quarks, each in three colors, coupling to massless gauge gluons. The quarks are confined within colorless hadrons by a long-range spin-independent force realizing infrared slavery. We use the asymptotic freedom of the model to argue that for the calculation of hadron masses, the short-range quark-quark interaction may be taken to be Coulomb-like. We rederive many successful quark-model mass relations for the low-lying hadrons. Because a specific interaction and symmetry-breaking mechanism are forced on us by the underlying renormalizable gauge field theory, we also obtain new mass relations. They are well satisfied. We develop a qualitative understanding of many features of the hadron mass spectrum, such as the origin and sign of the $\ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{-}\ensuremath{\Lambda}$ mass splitting. Interpreting the newly discovered narrow boson resonances as states of charmonium, we use the model to predict the masses of charmed mesons and baryons.
summary:
Physics Paper Predicts Charmined Masses using Standard Gauge Model

A groundbreaking physics paper by A. De Rújula, Howard Georgi, and Sheldon L. Glashow in Physical Review D suggests a new understanding of hadron masses through the "standard" gauge model, which includes four types of fractionally charged quarks and massless gauge gluons. The paper argues that for the calculation of hadron masses, the short-range quark-quark interaction can be approximated as Coulomb-like due to the model's asymptotic freedom.

Using this approach, the researchers rederive successful quark-model mass relations for low-lying hadrons and predict new ones that are well-satisfied. Additionally, they offer a qualitative understanding of various features in the hadron mass spectrum, such as the origin and sign of the $\ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{-}\ensuremath{\Lambda}$ mass splitting.

The researchers also apply their model to newly discovered narrow boson resonances, interpreting them as states of charmonium, and predict the masses of charmed mesons and baryons. Their work provides insight into the underlying structure of hadrons and sets the stage for further exploration in particle physics.

title: Cosmology
abstract: Abstract This book is unique in the detailed, self-contained, and comprehensive treatment that it gives to the ideas and formulas that are used and tested in modern cosmological research. It divides into two parts, each of which provides enough material for a one-semester graduate course. The first part deals chiefly with the isotropic and homogeneous average universe; the second part concentrates on the departures from the average universe. Throughout the book the author presents detailed analytic calculations of cosmological phenomena, rather than just report results obtained elsewhere by numerical computation. The book is up to date, and gives detailed accounts of topics such as recombination, microwave background polarization, leptogenesis, gravitational lensing, structure formation, and multifield inflation, that are usually treated superficially if at all in treatises on cosmology. Copious references to current research literature are supplied. Appendices include a brief introduction to general relativity, and a detailed derivation of the Boltzmann equation for photons and neutrinos used in calculations of cosmological evolution. Also provided is an assortment of problems.

title: Reheating after Inflation
abstract:
The theory of reheating of the Universe after inflation is developed. The
transition from inflation to the hot Universe turns out to be strongly
model-dependent and typically consists of several stages. Immediately after
inflation the field $\phi$ begins rapidly rolling towards the minimum of its
effective potential. Contrary to some earlier expectations, particle production
during this stage does not lead to the appearance of an extra friction term
$\Gamma\dot\phi$ in the equation of motion of the field $\phi$. Reheating
becomes efficient only at the next stage, when the field $\phi$ rapidly
oscillates near the minimum of its effective potential. We have found that
typically in the beginning of this stage the classical inflaton field $\phi$
very rapidly (explosively) decays into $\phi$-particles or into other bosons
due to broad parametric resonance. This stage cannot be described by the
standard elementary approach to reheating based on perturbation theory. The
bosons produced at this stage, as well as some part of the classical field
$\phi$ which survives the stage of explosive reheating, should further decay
into other particles, which eventually become thermalized. The last stages of
decay can be described in terms of perturbation theory. Complete reheating is
possible only in those theories where a single massive $\phi$-particle can
decay into other particles. This imposes strong constraints on the structure of
inflationary models. On the other hand, this means that a scalar field can be a
cold dark matter candidate even if it is strongly coupled to other fields.
summary:
"Physicists propose new theory on Universe's reheating after inflation

A team led by scientists Lev Kofman, Andrei Linde, and Alexei A. Starobinsky challenges the conventional understanding of how the Universe transitioned from an inflating state to a hot one. The study introduces a series of stages in this reheating process.

Unlike previous assumptions, the researchers found that particle production during the initial stage does not introduce an additional friction term into the equation of motion for the field $\phi$. Efficient reheating occurs only at a subsequent phase, when $\phi$ rapidly oscillates near its effective potential's minimum. This rapid decay of classical inflaton field $\phi$ is said to result in a 'explosive' production of $\phi$-particles or other bosons due to broad parametric resonance."

title: <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>CPT</mml:mi></mml:math>violation and the standard model
abstract:
Spontaneous CPT breaking arising in string theory has been suggested as a
possible observable experimental signature in neutral-meson systems. We provide
a theoretical framework for the treatment of low-energy effects of spontaneous
CPT violation and the attendant partial Lorentz breaking. The analysis is
within the context of conventional relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum
field theory in four dimensions. We use the framework to develop a
CPT-violating extension to the minimal standard model that could serve as a
basis for establishing quantitative CPT bounds.

Title: New Physics Frontier: Proposed Framework for Detecting CPT Violation in Particle Systems

In an exciting development, physicists Don Colladay and V. Alan Kostelecký have published a groundbreaking paper in the Physical Review journal exploring the potential for observable experimental signatures of CPT violation in neutral-meson systems. The study delves into the low-energy effects of spontaneous CPT violation and related partial Lorentz breaking, using conventional relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum field theory in four dimensions. This work could pave the way for establishing new bounds on CPT symmetry, a critical principle in physics that ensures the conservation of energy, momentum, and charge during any physical transformation. The researchers propose a CPT-violating extension to the standard model, offering a potential basis for future experimental testing of these intriguing ideas.

abstract: Proton NMR chemical shift and J-coupling values are presented for 35 metabolites that can be detected by in vivo or in vitro NMR studies of mammalian brain.
